claims.rationale: Every phonological segment, stress placement, spelling alternation (-ey/-y, Mi-/Ma-/Mu-), and early capitalization pattern of American malarkey is accounted for directly by Anglicized Mullarkey/Malarkey remodeled on synonymous Hiberno-English blarney, without requiring unattested monolingual Gaelic or foreign borrowings.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Exact phonological identity (/məˈlɑːrki/) with the Anglicized Connacht surname Mullarkey/Malarkey, continuous 1890–1927 stage-Irish comic stereotyping linking the surname to blarney and hot-air boasting, and persistent capital M- in 1922–1930 slang witnesses.

claims.target_lexeme: malarkey, n. (scholarly Irish Gaelic *meallaireacht and mullachán proposals)
claims.case_section: 4. Phonological Donor Matrix, Folk-Myth Refutations, and Trap A–D Audit
claims.short_label: Evaluation weakening Sayers's (2002) Irish *meallaireacht and Green's mullachán donor proposals
claims.statement: Primary-lexicon inspection of Patrick S. Dinneen's Foclóir Gaedhilge agus Béarla (1904, pp. 473, 502) leaves two serious scholarly Irish common-noun proposals—William Sayers's (Western Folklore 61, 2002) hypothetical abstract noun *meallaireacht (< meallaire 'deceiver', mealladh 'beguiling') and Jonathon Green's tentative comparison with mullachán ('peak; big-headed boy')—unsubstantiated as primary donors: Dinneen records only mealltóireacht (with medial -t-) rather than *meallaireacht, neither Irish word contains medial /-rk-/ with velar stop /k/, and 1920s American sportswriters lacked monolingual Irish lexical contact outside the Anglicized surname.
claims.rationale: Auditing Dinneen (1904) directly tests Sayers's peer-reviewed conjecture and Green's tentative comparison with appropriate scholarly respect, grading them inconclusive on phonological and attestation gaps while separating them strictly from fabricated pseudo-Gaelic claims.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Absence of unstarred *meallaireacht in Dinneen (1904, p. 473, which attests meallaire and mealltóireacht) and phonological mismatch between Irish /-lˠəɾʲəxt̪ˠ/ or [ˈmˠʊlˠəxɑːnˠ] and English /-ˈlɑːrki/.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Impossibility of secondary semantic resonance among bilingual Irish-American speakers already familiar with the surname Mullarkey.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether 19th-century Connacht or Munster oral Irish ever formed *meallaireacht without -t- and adapted -acht to English -key in immigrant speech.

limitations: Per DRAgNEt scholarly register discipline, Sayers (2002) and Green are serious philological proposals evaluated as weakened/inconclusive rather than 'falsified myths'.
resolution_criteria: Attest unstarred Irish meallaireacht in pre-1922 Irish texts AND document a pre-1923 Hiberno-English phonetic bridge exhibiting rhotic /-rk-/ and final /-i/.

evidence.reason: Verifies on Dinneen (1904) pp. 473 and 502 that meallaire ('deceiver') and mealltóireacht are attested while *meallaireacht is absent, and mullachán means 'peak, hillock; large-headed boy'.
References William Sayers's 2002 Western Folklore article engaging Peter Tamony's San Francisco malarkey files.
Contrasts hypothetical Gaelic common-noun adaptation with the already existing, segmentally exact Anglicized surname Mullarkey/Malarkey.

claims.target_lexeme: marlock / malack / marlocky (Northern English dialect) and Priestley's 1929 'malachin' abart'
claims.case_section: 4. Phonological Donor Matrix, Folk-Myth Refutations, and Trap A–D Audit
claims.short_label: Northern English marlock/malack evaluation and reclassification of Priestley's 1929 'malachin' abart'
claims.statement: Primary scans of John Collier (1757, Marlocks 'awkward gestures, tricks'), Nodal & Milner's Lancashire Glossary (1875, MARLOCK 'playful trick, prank, frolic'), and Joseph Wright's English Dialect Dictionary (Vol. IV, 1903/1905, Yorkshire/Lincolnshire non-rhotic malack 'fraudulent contrivance or trick' and Marlocky 'frolicsome', correcting Wiltshire misattributions) establish Northern English marlock/malack as a plausible secondary reinforcement only if remodeled onto amphibrachic Malarkey/blarney, while proving that J. B. Priestley's 1929 Good Companions 'malachin' abart' (listed under malarkey, v. in Green's Dictionary of Slang) is actually West Yorkshire dialectal malackin' (< marlock).
claims.rationale: Inspecting Wright's EDD (1903/1905) accomplishes two things simultaneously: it bounds marlock/marlocky's initial stress ['mɑː(r)ləki] against American [məˈlɑːrki], and it resolves the anomalous 1929 Yorkshire verb citation in Green's Dictionary of Slang as regional malackin' ('playing the fool').

evidence_boundary.establishes: 1757–1905 Northern English dialect attestation of marlock / malack ('prank, fraudulent trick') and Marlocky ('frolicsome'), absence from Dartnell & Goddard's 1893 Wiltshire Glossary, and dialectal identity of Priestley's 1929 'malachin' abart'.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Standalone derivation of American malarkey from Lancashire/Yorkshire marlock without stress-shift remodeling onto the surname Malarkey.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether 19th-century Lancashire/Yorkshire immigrants in American sporting circles blended 'marlocky' into 'Malarkey' speech play.

limitations: CERT-2700-305 inspects the 1905 set reissue of Wright's EDD Vol. IV (originally issued 1903; cataloged '1898' on Internet Archive).
resolution_criteria: Locate pre-1923 American dialect or sporting-press attestations of 'marlock' / 'marlocky' transitioning to second-syllable stress or 'nonsense talk' semantics.

evidence.reason: Supplies John Collier's ('Tim Bobbin') 1757 Lancashire glossary entry 'Marlocks, awkward Gestures; also foolish Tricks'.
Supplies Nodal & Milner's 1875 Lancashire Glossary entry 'MARLOCK, a playful trick, a prank, a game, a frolic'.
Supplies Wright's EDD Vol. IV (1903/1905) entries for non-rhotic Yorkshire/Lincolnshire 'malack' ('fraudulent contrivance') and 'Marlocky', plus Dartnell & Goddard's 1893 Wiltshire Glossary check.
evidence.witness_note: Edition state noted: 1905 set reissue of 1903 Vol. IV.

evidence.reason: Records Green's Dictionary of Slang's citation of J. B. Priestley's 1929 Good Companions ('malachin' abart') under malarkey, v., here reclassified as West Yorkshire malackin'.

claims.target_lexeme: malarkey, n. (proposed Modern Greek μαλακία donor and Beale's 'Madame Misharty')
claims.case_section: 4. Phonological Donor Matrix, Folk-Myth Refutations, and Trap A–D Audit
claims.short_label: Phonological and semantic evaluation weakening Partridge's Modern Greek μαλακία proposal
claims.statement: Primary-lexicon audit of Liddell & Scott (1883, μαλακία 'softness, effeminacy, sickness') and Achilleus Kyriakides's Modern Greek-English Dictionary (2nd ed., Athens, 1909, p. 442: μαλακία strictly anatomical 'masturbation; onanism; self-abuse', μαλάκα 'softening of the brain'), synthesized with Quinion (2006) and Liberman (2007), leaves Eric Partridge's Modern Greek conjecture and Paul Beale's London fortune-teller phrase 'Madame Misharty' unsubstantiated: Greek μαλακία [malaˈcia] is non-rhotic, carries penult /-ˈki-/ stress, lacked a documented pre-1922 'empty talk/bunk' sense, and was register-incompatible with 1922 family newspaper comics.
claims.rationale: Checking Kyriakides (1909) directly establishes the exact pre-World War I Modern Greek lexical meaning and prosody, explaining why mainstream etymologists view Partridge's Greek conjecture as unlikely while retaining an inconclusive open gate should pre-1922 Greek-American diner/port slang evidence ever emerge.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Exact 1883 Classical and 1909 Modern Greek dictionary definitions and non-rhotic [malaˈcia] prosody of μαλακία, demonstrating severe semantic, register, and phonological distance from 1922–1923 American sports/comic malarkey.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absolute impossibility of undocumented oral Greek-American urban slang bleaching prior to 1922.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: When colloquial Modern Greek bleached μαλακίες ('masturbations') to conversational 'nonsense, rubbish' in 20th-century Greek immigrant speech.

limitations: CERT-2700-306 pairs Liddell & Scott (7th ed., 1883) and Kyriakides (2nd ed., 1909) on a composite lexical audit plate; per scholarly register rules, Partridge's proposal is graded inconclusive rather than a falsified myth.
resolution_criteria: Locate pre-1922 Greek-American or Mediterranean port print attesting μαλακία / malakia in the bleached sense 'boastful talk, nonsense' with rhotic English adaptation.

evidence.reason: Verifies in Liddell & Scott (1883, p. 916) and Kyriakides (1909, p. 442) that pre-1922 Modern Greek μαλακία meant strictly 'masturbation; self-abuse' with non-rhotic penult stress.
evidence.witness_note: Composite lexical scan pairing 1883 Liddell-Scott and 1909 Kyriakides.

evidence.reason: Summarizes Quinion's (World Wide Words) phonological and sociolinguistic critique of Partridge's Greek μαλακία and Beale's London 'Madame Misharty' conjectures.

Stephen Mullarky rather than continuous generic slang, while independently illustrating the surname's comic transparency to muddle/lark wordplay.
